report.source_text: Intravenous ceftazidime three times a day with oral co-trimoxazole (160 mg/800 mg) one tablet two times a day was started. Fucibet cream (a combined topical potent corticosteroid and fusidic acid), along with various wound dressings were used with no significant effect. Once a diagnosis of CM was made, the dose of co-trimoxazole was increased to the recommended (160 mg/800 mg) two tablets two times a day with folic acid supplementation for 3 months. The topical corticosteroid was stopped. Our specialist dermatology nurse debrided and dressed the wound with a negative pressure dressing on a weekly basis for several weeks. The patient was then taught how to manage the negative pressure dressing.

report.source_text: An incisional skin biopsy was taken and the histology demonstrated ulceration and an acanthotic epithelium, overlying a deep dermal inflammatory infiltrate comprising of neutrophils, lymphocytes, histiocytes and plasma cells (figure 2). There was no evidence of granulomas, vasculitis, malignancy or viral inclusions. Gram, DPAS, Grocott, Giemsa, Ziehl-Neelson and Wade-Fite special stains were all negative. The histological features were non-specific. Tissue bacterial and fungal cultures produced no significant growth, and Lesihmania PCR was negative.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Cutaneous melioidosis caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 26-year-old man with extensive travel through Southeast Asia (Thailand, Nepal, India) presented with a 3-month history of progressive left leg ulceration that began as an erythematous lesion on the lateral lower leg near the lateral malleolus, attributed to an insect bite in Thailand. The lesion enlarged and ulcerated despite multiple courses of oral antibiotics in Nepal and India, with two additional adjacent ulcers developing on the anterior and medial lower leg. The patient remained systemically well without fever, lymphadenopathy, or organ dysfunction. Multiple initial wound swabs did not isolate a pathogen, but one swab from the referring hospital grew an organism initially identified as Burkholderia thailandensis by standard methodology. However, the organism's unusual antibiotic susceptibility profile made B. pseudomallei a more likely culprit. The diagnosis of cutaneous melioidosis caused by B. pseudomallei was made on clinical and microbiological grounds. MRI of the left leg ruled out tendinopathy and osteomyelitis. Incisional skin biopsy showed ulceration with deep dermal inflammatory infiltrate (neutrophils, lymphocytes, histiocytes, plasma cells) but no granulomas, vasculitis, or organisms on special stains; tissue cultures were negative. Treatment was initiated with intravenous ceftazidime three times daily and oral co-trimoxazole (160 mg/800 mg) one tablet twice daily. After diagnosis confirmation, co-trimoxazole was escalated to two tablets twice daily with folic acid supplementation for 3 months, and topical corticosteroid was discontinued. Weekly wound debridement and negative pressure dressing were applied for several weeks, then managed by the patient. Within 3 weeks of higher-dose co-trimoxazole and negative pressure dressing, the ulcers re-epithelialized with scarring. There was no recurrence of skin lesions 20 months after stopping oral co-trimoxazole.

final.final_diagnosis: Cutaneous melioidosis caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei
final.trajectory_summary: A 26-year-old man with extensive travel through Southeast Asia (Thailand, Nepal, India) presented with a 3-month history of progressive left leg ulceration that began as an erythematous lesion on the lateral lower leg near the lateral malleolus, attributed to an insect bite in Thailand. The lesion enlarged and ulcerated despite multiple courses of oral antibiotics in Nepal and India, with two additional adjacent ulcers developing on the anterior and medial lower leg. The patient remained systemically well without fever, lymphadenopathy, or organ dysfunction. Multiple initial wound swabs did not isolate a pathogen, but one swab from the referring hospital grew an organism initially identified as Burkholderia thailandensis by standard methodology. However, the organism's unusual antibiotic susceptibility profile made B. pseudomallei a more likely culprit. The diagnosis of cutaneous melioidosis caused by B. pseudomallei was made on clinical and microbiological grounds. MRI of the left leg ruled out tendinopathy and osteomyelitis. Incisional skin biopsy showed ulceration with deep dermal inflammatory infiltrate (neutrophils, lymphocytes, histiocytes, plasma cells) but no granulomas, vasculitis, or organisms on special stains; tissue cultures were negative. Treatment was initiated with intravenous ceftazidime three times daily and oral co-trimoxazole (160 mg/800 mg) one tablet twice daily. After diagnosis confirmation, co-trimoxazole was escalated to two tablets twice daily with folic acid supplementation for 3 months, and topical corticosteroid was discontinued. Weekly wound debridement and negative pressure dressing were applied for several weeks, then managed by the patient. Within 3 weeks of higher-dose co-trimoxazole and negative pressure dressing, the ulcers re-epithelialized with scarring. There was no recurrence of skin lesions 20 months after stopping oral co-trimoxazole.
